case.case_title: Deshapriya v. Rukmani, Divisional Secretary, Dodangoda and Others

clause.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation or business.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the suspension of the petitioner, a Samurdhi Niyamaka, infringed his fundamental right under Article 14(1)(g) relating to freedom to engage in lawful occupation.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that his lawful occupation was affected by the suspension, constituting an infringement of Article 14(1)(g).
case_context.respondent_argument: No distinct or independent act or omission constituting an infringement of Article 14(1)(g) was suggested; the suspension was a consequence of acts infringing Article 12.
key_facts: The petitioner was suspended from his position as a Samurdhi Niyamaka without reason.
The suspension followed the petitioner's refusal to canvass for certain political candidates.
The suspension was found to be an infringement of Articles 12(1) and 12(2).
No separate or independent violation of Article 14(1)(g) was established.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that although the petitioner's lawful occupation was affected by the suspension, this was entirely due to infringements of Article 12 rights. There was no evidence of a separate violation of Article 14(1)(g).
reasoning.application_to_facts: Since the suspension was unlawful under Article 12, any impact on the petitioner's occupation was consequential, not a direct violation of Article 14(1)(g).
principles_established: Impact on lawful occupation caused by infringement of other fundamental rights does not independently establish a violation of Article 14(1)(g).
Separate and distinct acts must be shown to claim infringement under Article 14(1)(g).

outcome.holding: The court found it unnecessary to consider whether the suspension violated Article 14(1)(g) as the petitioner’s rights under Article 12 were infringed and relief granted on that basis would fully redress the injury.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: The petitioner claimed infringement of Article 14(1)(g) due to suspension affecting his occupation, but the court ruled that the impact was a consequence of violations of Article 12 rights, making separate consideration of Article 14(1)(g) unnecessary.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: While it is true that the petitioner's lawful occupation was affected by the suspension of his services, nevertheless, that was entirely the consequence of acts which - as I now hold - were infringements of Article 12. There is no suggestion that there was any other distinct or independent act or omission constituting an infringement of Article 14 (1) (g). Consequently, whatever wrong or injury the petitioner suffered will be fully redressed by granting him relief in respect of his claims under Article 12.
